q: For its 2025 tax year, Domco, a U.S. C corporation, owns 100% of one CFC with $1,000,000 of tested income, $2,000,000 of qualified business asset investment (QBAI) and no tested interest expense. Under the GILTI rules then in effect (net deemed tangible income return of 10% of QBAI), what is Domco's GILTI inclusion before any §78 gross-up?
exp: GILTI = net CFC tested income minus net deemed tangible income return: $1,000,000 - (10% x $2,000,000) = $800,000. The $400,000 trap applies the 50% §250 deduction, which reduces taxable income but not the inclusion itself.

q: For 2025, Domco has a $900,000 GILTI inclusion, an inclusion percentage of 100%, and $100,000 of foreign income taxes attributable to tested income. Assume a 50% §250 deduction, a 21% rate, deemed-paid credit equal to 80% of the attributable taxes, and no expense allocation (the §904 limitation does not bind). What is Domco's net U.S. tax on the GILTI?
exp: Inclusion plus §78 gross-up = $1,000,000; after the 50% §250 deduction, $500,000 x 21% = $105,000, less an FTC of 80% x $100,000 = $80,000, leaves $25,000. The $14,500 trap omits the §78 gross-up.

q: Assume that for tax years beginning after 2025 the GILTI regime (renamed net CFC tested income, NCTI) has no QBAI reduction, a §250 deduction of 40%, and a deemed-paid credit of 90% of attributable foreign taxes. In 2026, Domco's NCTI is $1,000,000 and attributable foreign taxes are $100,000 (inclusion percentage 100%, limitation not binding, 21% rate). What is Domco's net U.S. tax on the NCTI?

For its 2025 tax year, ExportCo has deduction eligible income of $1,000,000, of which $600,000 is foreign-derived, and QBAI of $2,000,000. Assume FDII = deemed intangible income (DEI minus 10% of QBAI) times the foreign-derived ratio, and a §250 FDII deduction of 37.5%. What is ExportCo's FDII deduction?
exp: Deemed intangible income = $1,000,000 - $200,000 = $800,000; FDII = $800,000 x ($600,000 / $1,000,000) = $480,000; and 37.5% x $480,000 = $180,000. The $225,000 trap applies 37.5% to the $600,000 of foreign-derived DEI without removing the deemed tangible return.

q: Worldco, a U.S. corporation, has worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, including $400,000 of foreign-source general-category taxable income. Its precredit U.S. tax is $210,000, and it paid $100,000 of foreign income taxes on the general-category income. What foreign tax credit may Worldco claim this year?
exp: The §904 limitation is $210,000 x ($400,000 / $1,000,000) = $84,000, which is less than the $100,000 paid, so the credit is $84,000. The $16,000 excess can be carried back 1 year and forward 10 years.

q: In 2025, a U.S. corporation's foreign income taxes deemed paid on its GILTI exceed its §904 limitation for the GILTI basket by $30,000. What happens to the $30,000?
choices: It is carried back 1 year and forward 10 years
It cannot be carried back or forward and is permanently lost
It may be deducted instead of credited in the same year
It may be used against general-category income
exp: Excess GILTI-basket credits have no carryback or carryforward under §904, so they are lost. The 1-back/10-forward rule applies only to other baskets, and income cannot be moved between baskets.

q: Sam, a single U.S. individual, has only passive foreign-source income, all reported on payee statements, with $250 of creditable foreign taxes withheld. Which statement about Sam's foreign tax credit is correct?
choices: He must file Form 1116 to claim any credit
He may only deduct the tax because it is under $300
He may elect to claim the full $250 credit without Form 1116 and without the §904 limitation
He may claim the credit only if he itemizes deductions
exp: The §904(j) de minimis election lets individuals with only passive income and creditable foreign taxes of $300 or less ($600 if married filing jointly) claim the credit without Form 1116 or the limitation. A credit, unlike a deduction, does not require itemizing.

q: SellCo, a CFC incorporated in Country X, buys products from its U.S. parent and resells them to unrelated customers in Country Y for use there. SellCo has no manufacturing activity. How is SellCo's sales profit classified?
choices: Tested income for GILTI only, because the customers are unrelated
Exempt because it is active business income
Foreign personal holding company income
Foreign base company sales income, a type of Subpart F income
exp: Buying from a related person and selling property made and used outside the CFC's country of incorporation is foreign base company sales income under §954. Unrelated customers do not prevent the classification, because the purchase was from a related party.

q: ForCo, a foreign corporation, is owned by the following unrelated persons (vote and value): Ann (U.S. citizen) 30%, Bix Corp. (U.S.) 25%, Carl (U.S. citizen) 9%, Dee (U.S. citizen) 8%, and a foreign individual 28%. ForCo has Subpart F income. Who must include a share of ForCo's Subpart F income?
choices: Ann and Bix Corp. only
Ann, Bix Corp., Carl and Dee
No one, because no U.S. person owns more than 50%
Ann only
exp: U.S. shareholders (10% or more) Ann and Bix together own 55%, which makes ForCo a CFC, and only U.S. shareholders include Subpart F income. Carl and Dee are under 10%, so they are not U.S. shareholders even though U.S. persons own 72% in total.

q: With a 21% U.S. corporate rate, a CFC may elect to exclude high-taxed income from Subpart F if the foreign effective tax rate exceeds 90% of the U.S. rate. Which foreign effective rate on a CFC's foreign base company income qualifies?
exp: The threshold is 90% x 21% = 18.9%, and only 19% exceeds it. The 18% rate is the trap: it is close to the threshold but below 18.9%.

q: USCo has owned 20% of a foreign corporation for three years. It receives a $500,000 foreign-source dividend (not a hybrid dividend) from undistributed non-PTEP earnings, with $50,000 of foreign withholding tax. What is the U.S. tax treatment?
choices: $500,000 is taxable with a $50,000 foreign tax credit
$500,000 is taxable with a $50,000 deduction for the withholding tax
A $500,000 §245A deduction applies, and the $50,000 withholding is neither creditable nor deductible
A 65% dividends-received deduction applies, with a credit for the withholding tax
exp: §245A gives a 100% DRD for the foreign-source portion of dividends from a specified 10%-owned foreign corporation when the holding period is met, and §245A denies both the credit and the deduction for related foreign taxes. The 65% DRD applies to domestic dividends, not this case.

q: Lia, a U.S. citizen, met the physical presence test for 300 days of 2025 (a 365-day year) and earned $150,000 of foreign wages during that period. Assume the 2025 maximum foreign earned income exclusion is $130,000. What is her foreign earned income exclusion?
exp: The exclusion is prorated by qualifying days: $130,000 x 300 / 365 = $106,849. Claiming the full $130,000 ignores the proration.

q: Assume for 2025 a $130,000 maximum foreign earned income exclusion, a housing base amount of 16% of that maximum ($20,800), and a housing expense cap of 30% of that maximum ($39,000) for Mark's foreign city. Mark qualifies for the full year, paid $40,000 of qualifying housing expenses, and his earned income is well above the exclusions. What is his foreign housing exclusion?
exp: Housing expenses are capped at $39,000, and the exclusion is $39,000 - $20,800 base = $18,200. The $19,200 trap subtracts the base from the uncapped $40,000.

q: A profitable U.S. corporation is entering a new foreign market and expects large operating losses for the first three years. If its goal is to use those losses against U.S. income as they occur, which structure is generally best?
choices: A foreign corporation treated as a corporation for U.S. tax purposes
A foreign branch or a foreign entity treated as disregarded under the check-the-box rules
A CFC whose losses offset Subpart F income of other CFCs
A domestic subsidiary that does not join the consolidated return
exp: Branch or disregarded-entity losses flow directly into the U.S. corporation's return. Losses of a foreign corporation stay inside it (a tested loss only offsets other CFCs' tested income), and a nonconsolidated subsidiary's losses stay with that subsidiary.

q: A newly formed foreign eligible entity has two members, each with limited liability under local law, and makes no entity classification election. What is its default U.S. tax classification?
choices: Partnership
Disregarded entity
Association taxable as a corporation
Trust
exp: Under Reg. §301.7701-3, a foreign eligible entity is a corporation by default if no member has unlimited liability. Partnership treatment is the default only if at least one member has unlimited liability, or under the domestic default rules.

q: USCo transfers appreciated equipment (FMV $900,000, basis $500,000) to its newly formed wholly owned foreign subsidiary in exchange for stock, in a transaction that would qualify under §351 if both corporations were domestic. How much gain does USCo recognize?
choices: $0, because §351 applies
$0 now, with gain deferred until the foreign subsidiary sells the equipment
Gain only to the extent of depreciation recapture
exp: §367 treats the foreign transferee as not being a corporation for nonrecognition purposes, so USCo recognizes the $400,000 gain on the outbound transfer of tangible property. Assuming §351 still applies is the trap.

q: A U.S. parent sells goods to its foreign distribution subsidiary, which resells them to unrelated customers for $1,000,000. Comparable independent distributors earn a 25% gross margin. Under the §482 resale price method, what is the arm's-length price the subsidiary pays the parent?
exp: Resale price minus the appropriate gross profit: $1,000,000 - (25% x $1,000,000) = $750,000. Treating 25% as a markup on cost ($1,000,000 / 1.25 = $800,000) confuses this method with cost plus.

q: USCo pays a $100,000 royalty for use of a patent in the United States to a foreign company resident in a treaty country. The treaty reduces the royalty withholding rate to 10%, and the payee gave USCo a valid Form W-8BEN-E claiming treaty benefits. How much must USCo withhold?
exp: Royalties are FDAP income subject to 30% withholding, reduced to the treaty rate (10% x $100,000 = $10,000) when the payee documents its eligibility. Without valid documentation, USCo would have to withhold $30,000.

q: A nonresident alien individual holds a registered bond issued by an unrelated U.S. corporation and owns no stock in the issuer. She provides a valid Form W-8BEN. What U.S. tax applies to the $40,000 of interest she receives?
choices: 30% withholding, or $12,000
Graduated rates as effectively connected income
None, under the portfolio interest exemption
15% FIRPTA withholding
exp: Portfolio interest paid to a documented foreign person who owns less than 10% of the issuer is exempt from U.S. tax under §871(h). FIRPTA applies only to U.S. real property interests.

q: A foreign individual sells a U.S. office building for $2,000,000. His adjusted basis is $1,200,000. Under the general FIRPTA withholding rule (§1445), how much must the buyer withhold?
exp: FIRPTA withholding is generally 15% of the amount realized, not the gain: 15% x $2,000,000 = $300,000. The $120,000 trap applies 15% to the $800,000 gain.

q: ForCorp, a foreign corporation, has $1,000,000 of effectively connected taxable income and pays $210,000 of U.S. income tax. Its U.S. net equity did not change during the year, and no treaty applies. What is ForCorp's branch profits tax?
exp: The dividend equivalent amount is effectively connected E&P of $1,000,000 - $210,000 = $790,000 (no change in net equity), and 30% x $790,000 = $237,000. The $300,000 trap applies 30% before subtracting the U.S. income tax.

q: For 2025, a U.S. corporation owns two CFCs. CFC 1 has tested income of $900,000 and QBAI of $1,000,000. CFC 2 has a tested loss of $300,000 and QBAI of $500,000. With no tested interest expense and a 10% deemed return on QBAI, what is the GILTI inclusion?
exp: Net tested income is $900,000 - $300,000 = $600,000, and only tested-income CFCs' QBAI counts: 10% x $1,000,000 = $100,000, so GILTI = $500,000. The $450,000 trap also counts the QBAI of the tested-loss CFC.

q: A U.S. corporation makes the GILTI high-tax exclusion election for a CFC whose tested income bears a foreign effective rate above 18.9%. What is a consequence of the election?
choices: The excluded income is taxed as Subpart F income instead
The foreign taxes on the excluded income may be carried forward 10 years
The excluded income is not tested income, and foreign taxes on it are not creditable
The CFC's QBAI is doubled in computing the deemed tangible return
exp: High-taxed income excluded from tested income produces no GILTI inclusion, so no deemed-paid credit is available for its foreign taxes. The election can also eliminate QBAI attributable to the excluded income, so it can reduce rather than increase the deemed return.

q: A U.S. distributor buys inventory from U.S. suppliers and sells it to customers in Germany, with title passing in Germany. The distributor does no manufacturing. What is the source of the sales income for foreign tax credit purposes?
choices: U.S. source, because the seller is a U.S. resident
Split 50/50 between U.S. and foreign source
U.S. source, because the inventory was purchased in the United States
Foreign source, because title passed outside the United States
exp: Gain on purchased inventory is sourced where title passes (§861 and §862), so it is foreign source. The 50/50 split was the old rule for inventory the seller produced, not purchased.

q: Jo, a U.S. consultant, received $200,000 for a project requiring 100 workdays, of which 40 days were worked in Canada and 60 in the United States. How much of the fee is foreign-source income?
exp: Compensation for personal services is sourced where the services are performed, so $200,000 x 40 / 100 = $80,000 is foreign source. Sourcing by the payer's residence or the taxpayer's citizenship is the trap.

q: Rhea, a U.S. individual, owns 15% of a CFC. Her CFC earned $300,000 of Subpart F income that she included in prior years. This year the CFC distributes $500,000 to her from its earnings, which total $800,000 including the $300,000 already taxed. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
exp: Distributions come first from previously taxed E&P, which is excluded under §959, so $300,000 is tax-free and the remaining $200,000 is a taxable dividend. As an individual, Rhea cannot claim the §245A deduction.

q: Tom, a U.S. citizen, had three foreign bank accounts during the year, with maximum balances (reached at different times) of $4,000, $3,500 and $3,000. What is his FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) filing obligation?
choices: None, because no single account exceeded $10,000
None, because the balances never exceeded $10,000 on the same day
He must file, because the aggregate of the accounts' maximum values ($10,500) exceeded $10,000
He must file only if the accounts earned more than $10,000 of income
exp: The FBAR threshold is an aggregate maximum value above $10,000 at any time during the year, computed by summing each account's maximum value: $4,000 + $3,500 + $3,000 = $10,500. The test does not look at individual accounts or a single day.

q: Pat, a U.S. citizen living in the U.K., is a U.K. resident under the U.S.-U.K. treaty tie-breaker rules. She argues the treaty exempts her U.K. wages from U.S. tax. What is the correct analysis?
choices: She is correct, because the treaty assigns taxing rights to her residence country
She is correct only if she files Form 8833
She is exempt only if U.K. tax exceeds U.S. tax
Under the treaty's saving clause, the United States may tax its citizens as if the treaty did not exist, although she may claim the FEIE or a foreign tax credit
exp: U.S. treaties contain a saving clause preserving U.S. taxation of citizens, so relief comes from the FEIE or the FTC rather than from treaty exemption. Form 8833 discloses treaty positions but cannot override the saving clause.

q: For 2025, which of the following is foreign-derived deduction eligible income of a U.S. C corporation for FDII purposes?
choices: Profit on a sale of equipment to an unrelated foreign customer for use outside the United States
GILTI inclusions from its CFCs
Profit on a sale to a U.S. wholesaler that later exports the goods
Income earned through its foreign branch
exp: FDDEI includes income from sales of property to foreign persons for foreign use and from services provided to persons located abroad. GILTI, Subpart F, dividends and foreign branch income are excluded from deduction eligible income, and a sale to a U.S. person for resale generally does not qualify.

q: Assume a 10% BEAT rate. A large U.S. corporation that meets the BEAT gross receipts and base erosion percentage thresholds has taxable income of $100 million after deducting $40 million of base erosion payments to foreign affiliates. Its regular tax liability, net of allowable credits, is $9 million. What is its BEAT liability?
choices: $14 million
$5 million
$4 million
exp: Modified taxable income = $100M + $40M = $140M, and 10% x $140M = $14M; BEAT is the excess over the $9M regular tax, or $5M. The $14M trap forgets to subtract the regular tax liability.

q: Assume a 2025 foreign earned income exclusion of $130,000. Nina earned $150,000 of foreign wages, excluded $130,000, and paid $30,000 of foreign income tax on the wages. Before applying the §904 limitation, how much of the foreign tax is eligible for credit?
exp: Foreign taxes allocable to excluded income are not creditable: $30,000 x $130,000 / $150,000 = $26,000 is disallowed, leaving $4,000. Claiming all $30,000 double-dips with the exclusion.

q: Assume a 2025 exclusion amount of $890,000 under §877A. Ron, a covered expatriate, renounces citizenship holding assets with $3,000,000 of unrealized gain (no deferred compensation or trust interests). What net gain does the mark-to-market regime treat as recognized?
exp: Under §877A, property is deemed sold the day before expatriation, and gain is reduced by the inflation-adjusted exclusion: $3,000,000 - $890,000 = $2,110,000. Expatriating does not avoid the exit tax.

q: USCo's wholly owned CFC earned $500,000 of pretax foreign base company income and paid $100,000 of foreign income tax on it. Assuming a 21% rate, no §250 deduction for Subpart F income, and the §904 limitation not binding, what is USCo's net U.S. tax on the Subpart F inclusion?
exp: Inclusion of $400,000 plus §78 gross-up of $100,000 = $500,000 x 21% = $105,000, less a full §960 deemed-paid credit of $100,000 = $5,000. The 80% haircut applies only to GILTI, not Subpart F.

q: A CFC has $30,000,000 of gross income, of which $1,200,000 is foreign base company income. Under the §954 de minimis rule, none of a CFC's gross income is treated as FBCI if FBCI is less than the lesser of 5% of gross income or $1,000,000. How much FBCI does the CFC have?
choices: $0, because FBCI is under 5% of gross income
exp: The de minimis threshold is the lesser of $1,500,000 (5%) or $1,000,000, so $1,000,000; because $1,200,000 exceeds it, all of the FBCI counts, not just the excess. The full-inclusion rule (all gross income) applies only when FBCI exceeds 70% of gross income.

q: Hal, a U.S. individual, owns 100% of a profitable foreign corporation that is a CFC generating large GILTI inclusions taxed at his 37% individual rate. Which planning election could most directly lower the current U.S. tax on the GILTI?
choices: Electing the foreign earned income exclusion
Electing to treat the CFC as a partnership
Making a §962 election to be taxed at corporate rates, with access to the §250 deduction and deemed-paid credits
Electing to deduct rather than credit foreign taxes
exp: A §962 election lets an individual U.S. shareholder be taxed on Subpart F and GILTI as if a domestic corporation, using the 21% rate, the §250 deduction and indirect credits, though later distributions are taxed again. The FEIE covers earned income only, not CFC inclusions.

q: EuroCo, a resident of a treaty country, sells goods to U.S. customers through an independent commission agent acting in the ordinary course of its own business, and has no U.S. office. Under the business profits article of a typical U.S. income tax treaty, how are EuroCo's U.S. sales profits treated?
choices: Taxed at 30% as FDAP income
Taxed as effectively connected income at 21%
Subject to the branch profits tax only
Not subject to U.S. income tax, because EuroCo has no U.S. permanent establishment
exp: Treaties allow the source country to tax business profits only if they are attributable to a permanent establishment, and an independent agent acting in its ordinary course does not create one. Business profits are not FDAP income.

q: USCo's foreign subsidiary pays several foreign levies. Which one is most likely creditable under §901 as a foreign income tax?
choices: Corporate income tax on net income, or a withholding tax imposed in lieu of an income tax
Value-added tax collected on the subsidiary's sales
A payroll tax for the local social security system on employer wages
A customs duty on imported components
exp: Creditable taxes are income taxes, or taxes in lieu of them under §903, such as withholding taxes on dividends or royalties. VAT, payroll and customs levies are not income taxes, though they may be deductible.

q: Why does a domestic corporation claiming a deemed-paid foreign tax credit for Subpart F or GILTI income include a §78 gross-up in income?
choices: To penalize income deferred offshore
To put the corporation in the same position as if it had earned the pretax foreign income directly and paid the foreign tax itself
To recapture foreign losses previously deducted
To convert the foreign tax into a deduction
exp: Without the gross-up, the corporation would be taxed on after-tax income while also crediting the tax, effectively getting both a deduction and a credit. §78 adds the deemed-paid taxes to income so the credit reflects pretax income.
